In health and social care settings, vulnerable people rely on safe meals to maintain health and wellbeing. Poor food hygiene can lead to outbreaks of foodborne illnesses, which can be severe or even fatal in people with weakened immune systems.
Effective food hygiene begins at the point of purchase and continues through storage, preparation, cooking and serving. Everyone involved in food handling must understand their responsibilities and follow local policies.

Foodborne illnesses are caused by consuming food or drink contaminated with harmful microorganisms or toxins. Common pathogens include bacteria (such as Salmonella, E. coli and Listeria), viruses (norovirus, hepatitis A) and parasites. Symptoms range from mild stomach upset to severe dehydration, organ damage or death.
Microorganisms multiply quickly in the right conditions: warmth, moisture, time and nutrients. Understanding the factors that allow bacteria to grow helps us prevent contamination and keep food safe.
People receiving care are more susceptible to foodborne illness. Keep hot foods above 63°C until served, and cool cooked foods quickly before refrigeration."},"meta":{"analyticsKey":"paragraph_5","tags":[],"aiHints":{"semanticRole":"","summary":"","difficulty":""}}},{"id":"90ededda-bcbd-426d-8397-7890cd0d5656","type":"rich_text","order":5,"payload":{"text":"Never leave perishable food at room temperature for more than two hours."},"meta":{"analyticsKey":"info_box_6","tags":[],"aiHints":{"semanticRole":"","summary":"","difficulty":""}}}],"metadata":{"locale":"en","readingMinutes":5,"tags":[],"aiReady":{"vectorizableText":"Safe Food Storage and Temperature Control
Correct storage stops food from spoiling or becoming contaminated. Temperature control is a key principle of food safety because it slows down or stops bacterial growth.
